Microsoft's third quarter saw positive market reaction as revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share surpassed Wall Street expectations. Management credited widespread adoption of its cloud and AI offerings—particularly Copilot and Foundry—for this performance, pointing to rapid growth in enterprise demand and expanded use cases across commercial and consumer segments. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted that "automated tasks have nearly doubled since July," with customer momentum translating into larger Copilot deployments and higher usage-based revenue.

Is now the time to buy MSFT? Find out in our full research report (it's free).

Microsoft (MSFT) Q3 CY2026 highlights:

Revenue $92.28 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $90.64 billion (1.8% beat)

EPS (GAAP) $4.92 vs analyst estimates of $4.72 (4.3% beat)

Gross margin 67.8%, down from 69% in the same quarter last year

Operating margin 49.8%, in line with the same quarter last year

Market capitalization $3.94 trillion

While we enjoy listening to the management's commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention.

Our top 5 analyst questions from Microsoft's Q3 earnings call

Adam Wood (Morgan Stanley) asked about the main drivers of long-term returns, focusing on infrastructure utilization versus monetizing more product layers. CEO Satya Nadella replied that margin improvements will come from both more efficient infrastructure and expanding monetization across products.

Karl Keirstead (UBS) inquired about the drivers behind Azure's projected growth. CFO Amy Hood explained that recent gains stem from engineering-driven efficiency, Foundry allocation, and higher token pricing, but noted variability in supply and usage-based pricing.

Mark Moerdler (Bernstein Research) questioned the mix of enterprise versus digitally native AI workloads. Nadella emphasized growing breadth of enterprise adoption, with examples from sectors like manufacturing and finance, and noted that enterprise-scale workloads are becoming the norm.

Brent Thill (Jefferies) asked if Microsoft can sustain high operating margins alongside rapid revenue growth. Hood responded that operational excellence, efficiency, and integrated product delivery are key to maintaining profitability.

Brad Reback (Stifel) probed the speed of adoption for usage-based billing outside of coding. Nadella acknowledged it will be faster in developer tools, while enterprise productivity solutions will require more gradual customer education and sales efforts.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) offered voluntary exits on October 26 to about 60,000 eligible employees. The offer covers select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below. That number counts the workers who qualify for the offer, since departures have yet to be confirmed, and for long-tenured U.S. employees considering the package, the costliest mistake could be hiding in the 401(k) paperwork.

PeopleImages / Shutterstock.com

Take Rick, a hypothetical 62-year-old eligible for the offer after 37 years at Microsoft. His 401(k) holds $1.2 million, including $250,000 in company stock acquired years ago. He could leave the money in Microsoft's plan after departing. But if he rolls the shares into an IRA without checking his options, he could permanently lose a valuable tax break.

How Old Company Shares Earn a Capital Gains Discount

Net unrealized appreciation (NUA) is the gain employer stock accumulated while it was held inside a retirement plan. Under a special federal tax rule, Rick can transfer qualifying Microsoft shares directly into a taxable brokerage account as part of a lump-sum distribution. He pays ordinary income tax on the cost basis, or what the plan originally paid for the shares. The appreciation isn't taxed until he sells, when it generally qualifies for long-term capital gains treatment.
